name: C++

facts.ai_role: The performance layer underneath the Python surface: PyTorch's libtorch, TensorFlow's core, CUDA kernels, llama.cpp, and most inference runtimes are C++.
facts.steward: ISO/IEC JTC1 SC22 WG21 standards committee

title: C++ in AI: The Performance Layer Beneath Python
answer: C++ is a compiled, general purpose programming language first released in 1985 and standardized by ISO/IEC JTC1 SC22 WG21. In AI work it is the performance layer beneath the Python surface: PyTorch's libtorch, TensorFlow's core, CUDA kernels, llama.cpp and most inference runtimes are C++. A reader deciding whether to use it should know that it buys speed and memory control at the cost of a steeper learning curve and manual resource management, and that it is usually paired with Python rather than replacing it.

sections.body: C++ is a compiled, general purpose programming language whose first release was in 1985, and it is stewarded by the ISO/IEC JTC1 SC22 WG21 standards committee rather than by a single company. The official site, isocpp.org, is run as the language's public home, carrying standardization news, meeting minutes, survey reports and conference announcements. In the AI stack it serves the performance layer underneath the Python surface. PyTorch's libtorch, TensorFlow's core, CUDA kernels, llama.cpp and most inference runtimes are written in C++, so the code a Python user calls into is frequently C++ all the way down. It sits below the modelling and scripting layers, where throughput, latency and memory layout matter more than iteration speed.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: The concrete AI jobs C++ does are the ones where the Python layer hands off: tensor and kernel execution inside frameworks, custom operators, model serving and inference runtimes, and edge or embedded deployment where a runtime must fit in constrained memory. The site's own material points to this role indirectly, through standardization work on std::simd and std::execution as standard library performance enhancers, and through committee study groups such as SG14 for low latency, games, embedded and financial trading, and SG19 for machine learning. It is strongest where space and time constraints are real, which is the framing the CppCon 2026 keynote summary uses when it cites industry data on demand for programmers who can work under such constraints. It is not presented on the site as the language for exploratory data analysis or notebook style experimentation.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: C++ has a reputation for a steep learning curve, and the official material supports that picture rather than softening it. The standardization pages describe a language that is still changing underfoot: C++20 is now the default in GCC 16.1, C++26 features such as reflection and contracts are arriving, and the committee has already voted the first additions into the working draft for C++29. A beginner benefits from prior programming experience, some understanding of how memory and hardware behave, and patience with toolchains, since even modules support in GCC 16.1 is still experimental and must be enabled explicitly. For mathematics, the site does not set out prerequisites, and the AI specific mathematical background is not covered there. What isocpp.org offers a newcomer is mostly secondary: survey reports, standards papers, meeting minutes and conference talk announcements, not a structured tutorial path.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: The ecosystem around C++ is large and largely external to the official site. isocpp.org documents the standards process itself: regular mailings of new standards papers, minutes from study groups including SG14 and SG19, trip reports from ISO meetings such as Kona and Brno, and annual developer surveys whose full write-in responses are forwarded to the committee and to tool vendors. Compiler vendors are visible through release news, for example GCC 16.1 shipping C++26 reflection, contracts and safety hardening. Conferences such as CppCon, held in Aurora, Colorado, with the 2026 edition starting September 12, act as the community's main gathering point, and the site promotes keynotes and talks there. Libraries, models and framework integrations are not catalogued on isocpp.org, so a developer looking for AI specific tooling will need sources beyond the official pages.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: C++ is built for production performance rather than quick experiments. The site's framing is consistently about efficiency, safety and control: std::simd and std::execution as performance enhancers, memory safety hardening in C++26, and draft profiles for stronger portable memory safety guarantees targeted at C++29. The cost of that control is visible in the same material. Compile times, toolchain configuration and feature availability vary by compiler and standard level, and some capabilities remain experimental, as with modules in GCC 16.1. The practical pattern is that teams prototype in a higher level language and then move hot paths, kernels or serving code into C++, which means the language is usually adopted for a specific bottleneck rather than for a whole project. The site does not present C++ as a rapid prototyping tool.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: The site supports the claim that C++ is a current standard rather than a legacy choice, though it does so through the lens of the standards process. The CppCon 2026 keynote summary states that the committee completed technical work on C++26 in March 2026 and voted the first C++29 additions in June, and it cites SlashData and IDC data on sustained demand for professional programmers, especially those who know languages that operate under real space and time constraints. The survey reports, now running to 100 and 145 pages with individual write-in responses, are sent to the committee and to product vendors, which indicates an active commercial constituency. The site does not publish adoption figures by industry or salary data, so anyone weighing C++ for a career should treat the official material as evidence of momentum and governance rather than as a market forecast.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: C++ is typically used with Python rather than against it. The pattern is a Python surface for orchestration, data handling and experimentation, with C++ underneath for kernels, operators, runtimes and serving, which is exactly the arrangement the facts describe for PyTorch's libtorch, TensorFlow's core, CUDA kernels, llama.cpp and most inference runtimes. Alongside C++ sit CUDA for GPU work and the framework specific extension mechanisms that let Python call compiled code. The site's own comparisons are narrower, mostly with Rust, as in a CppCon 2025 talk on JSON serialization and in the reflective metaprogramming work built on an experimental Bloomberg LLVM fork. That polyglot pattern, high level language for iteration and C++ for the constrained path, is the one most AI teams actually run.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: The official material is candid about what is unfinished. Memory safety is being addressed through hardening and draft profiles rather than solved, with profiles still being prototyped and targeted at C++29. Undefined behavior is only now getting a complete catalogue in the C++29 working draft, described as a first step toward systematic rather than piecemeal fixes. Modules support remains experimental in GCC 16.1. The site does not say how quickly these features will reach mainstream compilers, how portable the safety profiles will prove across vendors, or how AI specific tooling will evolve. It also does not cover AI libraries, benchmarks or deployment guidance, and it offers no structured beginner curriculum. Questions about which C++ standard a given AI runtime requires, or how much of a typical training pipeline is C++, are not settled by these pages.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
